proof:
# Discrete log-concave moments and a universal product inequality

The scalar theorem here is complete. Its transfer to unequal two-positive simplex caps uses a separate exact geometric reduction being independently audited. It does not resolve OC.

## 1. A finite discrete moment bound

Let N be a random variable supported on {0,...,m}, with a log-concave probability sequence positive throughout that interval. Put mu=E N. For every integer r>=1,

    E binom(N,r) <= mu^r.                              (1)

Consequently, whenever t>=0 and t mu<1,

    E(1+t)^N <= 1/(1-t mu).                            (2)

If mu>0 and t>0, inequality (2) is strict.

Proof. Write p_j=Pr(N=j), T_k=Pr(N>=k), with T_0=1 and T_k=0 beyond the support. Log-concavity makes p_(k+l)/p_k nonincreasing in k for each l>=0 wherever defined, by multiplying decreasing consecutive ratios. Thus T_k/p_k=sum_(l>=0)p_(k+l)/p_k is nonincreasing. The hazard p_k/T_k is nondecreasing, so T_(k+1)/T_k=1-p_k/T_k is nonincreasing. Therefore

    T_(a+b)<=T_a T_b

for nonnegative integers a,b, by multiplying tail ratios; zero tails cause no exception. Iterating this and using the tail identity for binomial moments gives

    E binom(N,r)
      =sum_(s>=r) binom(s-1,r-1) T_s
      =sum_(k_1,...,k_r>=1) T_(k_1+...+k_r)
      <=(sum_(k>=1)T_k)^r=mu^r.

All sums of tails are nonnegative and finite or monotone convergent, so rearrangement is justified. Expanding the finite binomial polynomial and comparing with the convergent geometric series proves (2). If mu,t>0, every sufficiently high geometric term is positive while the corresponding binomial moment is zero, proving strictness. The degenerate variable N=0 satisfies equality and is separately included.

## 2. The universal product theorem

For any m>=1 and x_1,...,x_m in (0,1), set

    rho=product_j(1-x_j), tau=rho/(1-rho),
    z=tau sum_j x_j.

Then 0<z<1 and

    (1-z) product_j(1+tau x_j) <= 1-rho z.            (3)

Equality holds when m=1; inequality is strict when m>=2.

Here is a proof with all changes of variables tracked. Put u_j=x_j/(1-x_j)>0 and let e_k be their elementary symmetric functions, including e_0=1. Write

    A=product_j(1+u_j)=sum_(k=0)^m e_k,
    E=A-1=sum_(k>=1)e_k,
    B=sum_(k>=1) k e_k,
    C=B-E=sum_(k>=1)(k-1)e_k.

Then rho=1/A, tau=1/E, and sum x_j=B/A. In particular

    1-z=(AE-B)/(AE)=(E^2-C)/(AE)>0.                  (4)

To justify the strict inequality in (4), expand E^2. Each squarefree monomial of degree k>=2 occurs with coefficient 2^k-2, whereas its coefficient in C is k-1. The former is greater. All nonsquarefree terms of E^2 are positive, and C has none. Thus E^2>C for positive u, including m=1 where C=0. Also z>0 directly.

Define a probability law by

    Pr(N=k-1)=e_k/E,  k=1,...,m.                     (5)

Its support is the full interval {0,...,m-1} and its mean is C/E. The elementary-symmetric coefficient sequence is log-concave. For a self-contained proof, form it by successive convolutions with (1,u_j). If a has contiguous positive support and is log-concave, b_l=a_l+u a_(l-1) obeys

    b_l^2-b_(l-1)b_(l+1)
      =(a_l^2-a_(l-1)a_(l+1))
       +u(a_l a_(l-1)-a_(l-2)a_(l+1))
       +u^2(a_(l-1)^2-a_(l-2)a_l)>=0.

The middle bracket is nonnegative by decreasing consecutive ratios; the endpoint-zero cases follow directly. Induction from (1) proves the claim. Truncating away e_0 and normalizing preserves log-concavity, so (5) satisfies Section 1.

To check the final algebra, put

    Q=product_j[E+A u_j]
      =sum_(k=0)^m e_k A^k E^(m-k).

Multiplying (3) by the positive number A^2 E^(m+1) shows it is equivalent to

    (AE-B)Q <= (A^2 E-B)E^m.                         (6)

Subtract the left side and cancel the positive factor A E^m. The resulting inequality is exactly

    E^2 >= (E^2-C) sum_(k=1)^m (e_k/E)(A/E)^(k-1),

or

    (1-C/E^2) E[(1+1/E)^N] <=1.                     (7)

Section 1 applies with t=1/E and mu=C/E because C<E^2. It proves (7), hence (3). For m>=2, C>0 and the finite-support strictness in (2) proves strictness. For m=1, N=0 and direct substitution gives equality.

## 3. The exact implication for an unequal-two-positive cap reduction

Suppose a separate geometric calculation has positive parameters h in (0,1), a_j in (0,1),

    rho=product_j(1-h a_j), L=h rho/(1-rho), S=sum_j a_j,

and the centrality condition LS>=1-h. Set x_j=h a_j. Then z in Section 2 is LS, and

    (1-LS) product_j(1+L a_j)
      <=1-rho LS <=1-(1-h)rho.                       (8)

This is precisely the proposed finite algebraic inequality in the unequal-two-positive reduction. The second inequality has the correct direction because LS>=1-h and rho>0. Thus no variational maximizer, limiting argument, or two-value classification is needed for that algebraic step. Identifying every geometric parameter and the desired cap-product ratio remains the responsibility of the separate transfer proof; equation (8) alone does not assert a statement for arbitrary cap incidences.
